# Exercise 2.3 — Cleaning and encoding {#sec-cleaning}

## Objectives

By the end of this exercise you will be able to:

- read a file and notice that two of its numeric columns arrived as text, and
  say why;
- convert inconsistent missing-value codes into real missing values;
- recognise one category recorded under three different spellings, and merge
  them;
- group a rare category into `Other`, and say what breaks if you do not;
- one-hot encode a categorical variable, count the columns it produces, and
  compare it with frequency encoding;
- state what happens when a category appears at prediction time that was never
  in the training data.

## Why this, here

Exercises 2.1 and 2.2 looked at distributions and at missingness in data that
was already numeric and already tidy. Real extracts are not. They arrive with
free-text categories typed by different people, with missing values recorded
three different ways in three different columns, and with columns that look
numeric until you try to take a mean.

This exercise and the three that follow all use **one small file**, so that
each exercise inherits the previous one's output. Nothing here uses a pipeline
or a recipe: every step is a plain function call, applied in the obvious order,
so that you can see what each one does. Exercise 2.6 then rebuilds the whole
sequence as a pipeline, and the comparison is the point.

## The extract

`clinic_extract.csv` is 150 rows, one per patient, with a binary `outcome`. It
is small deliberately — small enough that you can print the whole thing and
find the problems by eye before writing any code to find them.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

clinic <- read_csv(
  "data/clinic_extract.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
dim(clinic)
```

## Python

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

clinic = pd.read_csv(
    "data/clinic_extract.csv"
)
clinic.shape
```
:::

### 1) Look at the column types first

Before any statistics, ask what type each column came in as. This is the step
that is almost always skipped.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
sapply(clinic, class)
```

## Python

```{python}
clinic.dtypes
```
:::

`age` and `bmi` are **text**, not numbers. `bp_systolic` is a number. All three
have missing values — the difference is only in how the missingness was
written down. An empty cell is understood by both languages as missing; the
strings `unknown` and `?` are not, so the whole column becomes text to
accommodate them.

Try to take a mean of it, and the two languages fail in different ways. Run
both — the difference matters more than either message.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
mean(clinic$bmi)
```

## Python

```{python}
#| error: true
clinic["bmi"].mean()
```
:::

Python **raises** and stops. R **warns** and hands back `NA`, which a script
will happily carry into the next calculation and the one after that. The loud
failure is the safer one. If you work in R, this is the argument for reading
warnings rather than scrolling past them.

### 2) Find out how missingness was recorded

Count the distinct non-numeric values in each suspect column rather than
assuming you know which codes are in use.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
for (col in c("age", "bmi", "bp_systolic")) {
  v <- suppressWarnings(
    as.numeric(clinic[[col]])
  )
  bad <- clinic[[col]][is.na(v)]
  bad[is.na(bad)] <- "<empty>"
  cat(col, ":", "\n")
  print(table(bad))
}
```

## Python

```{python}
for col in ["age", "bmi", "bp_systolic"]:
    v = pd.to_numeric(
        clinic[col], errors="coerce"
    )
    bad = clinic[col][v.isna()]
    print(col, dict(
        bad.fillna("<empty>")
           .value_counts()
    ))
```
:::

Three columns, three conventions: `unknown`, `?`, and an empty cell. That is
not unusual — it usually means three people, or three systems, contributed to
the same table.

### 3) Convert the codes into real missing values

`to_numeric(errors="coerce")` and `as.numeric()` both turn anything they cannot
parse into a proper missing value. That is exactly what you want here, but only
because you have just checked what the unparseable values are. Coercing
blindly would silently destroy a column recorded in, say, `12,5` decimal-comma
format.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
num_cols <- c("age", "bmi", "bp_systolic")
clinic <- clinic |>
  mutate(across(
    all_of(num_cols),
    ~ suppressWarnings(as.numeric(.x))
  ))
colSums(is.na(clinic[num_cols]))
```

## Python

```{python}
num_cols = ["age", "bmi", "bp_systolic"]
for c in num_cols:
    clinic[c] = pd.to_numeric(
        clinic[c], errors="coerce"
    )
clinic[num_cols].isna().sum()
```
:::

Now a mean works, and `bmi` can be plotted. Keep that count of missing values
in mind — Exercise 2.4 is about what to do with them.

### 4) One category, three spellings

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
table(clinic$referral_source)
```

## Python

```{python}
clinic["referral_source"].value_counts()
```
:::

Five categories are reported. There are really three: `GP`, `gp` and
`General Practitioner` are one referral source typed by three different people.
Left alone, one-hot encoding would spend three columns on it and split its
effect three ways, so each fragment looks weaker than the source really is.

The repair is a lookup from the messy value to the intended one. Write it
explicitly rather than lower-casing and hoping — lower-casing fixes `gp` but
not `General Practitioner`.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
clinic <- clinic |>
  mutate(referral_source = recode(
    referral_source,
    "gp" = "GP",
    "General Practitioner" = "GP"
  ))
table(clinic$referral_source)
```

## Python

```{python}
ref_map = {
    "GP": "GP",
    "gp": "GP",
    "General Practitioner": "GP",
    "A&E": "A&E",
    "Self-referral": "Self-referral",
}
clinic["referral_source"] = (
    clinic["referral_source"].map(ref_map)
)
clinic["referral_source"].value_counts()
```
:::

### 5) A rare category

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
sort(table(clinic$hospital_site),
     decreasing = TRUE)
```

## Python

```{python}
clinic["hospital_site"].value_counts()
```
:::

One site has only a handful of patients. Keep it as its own category and you
get a column that is almost all zeros, estimated from those few rows — and if
an 80/20 split happens to put all of them on one side, the column is constant
in training and meaningless in test.

Grouping it into `Other` is the usual repair. Note what the threshold is doing:
it is a judgement about how many rows you need before you are willing to
estimate an effect, not a fact about the data.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
counts <- table(clinic$hospital_site)
rare <- names(counts[counts < 10])
clinic <- clinic |>
  mutate(hospital_site = if_else(
    hospital_site %in% rare,
    "Other", hospital_site
  ))
sort(table(clinic$hospital_site),
     decreasing = TRUE)
```

## Python

```{python}
counts = clinic["hospital_site"].value_counts()
rare = counts[counts < 10].index
clinic["hospital_site"] = (
    clinic["hospital_site"]
    .where(~clinic["hospital_site"].isin(rare),
           "Other")
)
clinic["hospital_site"].value_counts()
```
:::

### 6) A column that says almost nothing

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
print(table(clinic$consented))
var(as.numeric(clinic$consented == "Y"))
```

## Python

```{python}
print(clinic["consented"].value_counts())
print(
    clinic["consented"]
    .eq("Y").astype(float).var()
)
```
:::

Nearly every row takes the same value, so its variance is close to zero. A
near-constant column cannot help a model separate one patient from another:
there is almost nothing to separate them by.

Note the word *almost*. Low variance is not the same as unimportance — a flag
that is rare but decisive, such as a positive result on a confirmatory test,
has low variance and high value. The right question is whether the handful of
rows that differ are rows you care about, not whether the variance clears a
threshold.

## Task 1 — Clean the categories

Starting from the raw file again, repair both categorical columns in one pass.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
raw = pd.read_csv("data/clinic_extract.csv")

raw["referral_source"] = raw["referral_source"].______(ref_map)

counts = raw["hospital_site"].______()
rare = counts[counts < ______].index
raw["hospital_site"] = raw["hospital_site"].where(
    ~raw["hospital_site"].isin(rare), "______"
)

print(raw["referral_source"].nunique())   # expect 3
print(raw["hospital_site"].nunique())     # expect 6
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The first blank is the method that replaces each value using a dictionary. The
second returns the frequency of each category. The threshold is the one used
above, and the last blank is the label everything rare is folded into.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
raw = pd.read_csv("data/clinic_extract.csv")

raw["referral_source"] = raw["referral_source"].map(ref_map)

counts = raw["hospital_site"].value_counts()
rare = counts[counts < 10].index
raw["hospital_site"] = raw["hospital_site"].where(
    ~raw["hospital_site"].isin(rare), "Other"
)

print(raw["referral_source"].nunique())
print(raw["hospital_site"].nunique())
```
:::
:::

## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
raw <- read_csv("data/clinic_extract.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

raw <- raw |>
  mutate(referral_source = recode(referral_source,
                                  "gp" = "______",
                                  "General Practitioner" = "______"))

counts <- table(raw$hospital_site)
rare <- names(counts[counts < ______])
raw <- raw |>
  mutate(hospital_site = if_else(hospital_site %in% rare, "______", hospital_site))

n_distinct(raw$referral_source)   # expect 3
n_distinct(raw$hospital_site)     # expect 6
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
`recode()` maps old value to new, so both of the first two blanks are the value
you want them to become. The threshold and the fold-everything-else-into label
are the same two used above.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
raw <- read_csv("data/clinic_extract.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

raw <- raw |>
  mutate(referral_source = recode(referral_source,
                                  "gp" = "GP",
                                  "General Practitioner" = "GP"))

counts <- table(raw$hospital_site)
rare <- names(counts[counts < 10])
raw <- raw |>
  mutate(hospital_site = if_else(hospital_site %in% rare, "Other", hospital_site))

n_distinct(raw$referral_source)
n_distinct(raw$hospital_site)
```
:::
:::
:::

## Encoding: turning categories into columns

A model takes numbers. `GP` is not a number, and encoding it as 1, `A&E` as 2
and `Self-referral` as 3 would assert that `Self-referral` is three times
whatever `GP` is, and that `A&E` sits exactly between them. One-hot encoding
avoids that by giving each category its own 0/1 column.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
enc <- model.matrix(
  ~ referral_source + hospital_site - 1,
  data = clinic
)
print(dim(enc))
head(enc, 3)
```

## Python

```{python}
enc = pd.get_dummies(
    clinic[["referral_source",
            "hospital_site"]],
    dtype=int
)
print(enc.shape)
enc.head(3)
```
:::

Two columns became several. Count them: that is the cost of one-hot encoding,
and it grows with the number of categories, not with the number of rows.

### Frequency encoding, for comparison

When a variable has many categories, one column each becomes unwieldy.
Frequency encoding replaces each category with how often it occurs — one
column instead of many.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
p <- prop.table(table(clinic$hospital_site))
freq <- unname(p[clinic$hospital_site])
head(freq, 5)
```

## Python

```{python}
freq = clinic["hospital_site"].map(
    clinic["hospital_site"]
    .value_counts(normalize=True)
)
freq.head(5)
```
:::

It is compact, and it throws information away: two sites of equal size become
the same number, indistinguishable from each other. Use it when cardinality
makes one-hot impractical, and know what you traded.

### The category you have never seen

Encoders learn their categories from the data they are fitted to. A site that
appears for the first time after the model is deployed is not in that list, and
the encoder has no column for it. Depending on the setting it will error, or
quietly produce a row of zeros — a patient who appears to be at no site at all.

This is the first hint of the problem Exercise 2.6 is about: **the encoder is
fitted**. It has learnt something from the data, which means it matters
enormously *which* data it learnt from.

## Task 2 — Encode, and count the cost

::: {.panel-tabset}
## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
before = clinic[["referral_source", "hospital_site"]].shape[1]
after = pd.get_dummies(
    clinic[["referral_source", "hospital_site"]], dtype=______
).shape[1]

print(before, "->", after)
print(clinic["referral_source"].nunique()
      + clinic["hospital_site"].______())   # should equal `after`
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The first blank makes the 0/1 columns integers rather than booleans. The second
is the method counting distinct categories — one column per category, so the
totals must agree.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
before = clinic[["referral_source", "hospital_site"]].shape[1]
after = pd.get_dummies(
    clinic[["referral_source", "hospital_site"]], dtype=int
).shape[1]

print(before, "->", after)
print(clinic["referral_source"].nunique()
      + clinic["hospital_site"].nunique())
```

Two columns become nine, one per category across the two variables. Nothing is
lost and nothing is implied about ordering; the cost is paid in width.
:::
:::

## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
before <- 2
after <- ncol(model.matrix(~ referral_source + hospital_site - ______,
                           data = clinic))

cat(before, "->", after, "\n")
cat(n_distinct(clinic$referral_source) + n_distinct(clinic$______), "\n")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The `- 1` in the formula is what suppresses the intercept and so gives one
column per category rather than one fewer. The last blank is the other
categorical column.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
before <- 2
after <- ncol(model.matrix(~ referral_source + hospital_site - 1,
                           data = clinic))

cat(before, "->", after, "\n")
cat(n_distinct(clinic$referral_source) + n_distinct(clinic$hospital_site), "\n")
```

Two columns become nine, one per category across the two variables. Drop the
`- 1` and you get eight: with an intercept in the model, one category per
variable is absorbed into it as the reference level.
:::
:::
:::

## Reflection

1. `age` and `bmi` arrived as text and `bp_systolic` did not, although all
   three had missing values. What would you add to your own loading code to
   catch this on a file you have never seen?
2. Merging three spellings of `GP` raised its count. Which direction does that
   move a coefficient estimated on it, and why?
3. You set the rare-category threshold at 10. On what grounds would you argue
   for 5, or for 25? What is the threshold really a statement about?
4. Frequency encoding gave one column where one-hot gave six. Name a question
   you could answer with the one-hot version and not with the frequency
   version.

## Stretch

### Stretch 1 — Find the defects without being told
Reload the raw file and, without looking back at this chapter, write the
shortest piece of code you can that flags every column needing attention:
columns typed as text that should be numeric, categories differing only by case
or spacing, and columns whose most common value covers more than 95% of rows.

### Stretch 2 — The unseen category, for real
Split the cleaned data 80/20. Fit `get_dummies` or `model.matrix` on the
training rows only, then try to apply the same encoding to the test rows.
Engineer the failure: arrange a split where a category present in test is
absent from training, and record exactly what each language does about it.

## What you can and cannot now claim

You can say the extract has been cleaned: the missing-value codes are real
missing values, one referral source is recorded once rather than three times,
the rare site is grouped, and the categorical columns are encoded as numbers a
model can take.

You cannot yet say anything about the missing values themselves. They are
still missing — 33 of the 150 rows have at least one gap, and every step you
have taken so far has left them exactly as they were. That is
@sec-imputation.

You also cannot claim any of this was done safely. Every repair above used the
whole dataset: the rare-category threshold, the frequency encoding and the list
of known categories were all computed from all 150 rows, including the rows you
will later hold out to test on. That is the subject of @sec-pipeline-steps.
